title: Ulefnersen Wins a Phase 3 Trial in FUS-ALS: What the Results Mean
description: Ulefnersen met its main goal in the Phase 3 FUSION trial for FUS-ALS (p = 0.0005). What was tested, what was reported, and what happens next.
summary: On September 22, 2026, Otsuka and Ionis announced that ulefnersen met the main goal of its Phase 3 FUSION trial in FUS-ALS, an inherited form of ALS. It is the first successful trial in this form of the disease. ALS still has no cure, and the results have not yet been published in a journal.

p: Otsuka Pharmaceutical and Ionis Pharmaceuticals reported that ulefnersen showed a statistically significant benefit over placebo in the Phase 3 FUSION trial (P = .0005). The main measure combined three things: time to death or permanent ventilation, time to rescue treatment, and change on the ALSFRS-R scale, a standard questionnaire that tracks everyday function.
The randomized, double-blind part of the trial lasted 72 weeks and was followed by an open-label extension, in which everyone can receive the drug.

FUS-ALS is a genetic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) caused by changes in the FUS gene. Ulefnersen belongs to a class of drugs called antisense medicines, which are designed to lower the production of a harmful protein. Tofersen (Qalsody), which is FDA approved for SOD1-ALS, uses the same general approach for a different gene.

ul: Secondary results were favorable, including lower blood levels of neurofilament light chain, a marker of nerve-cell damage, and better combined time-to-event outcomes.
Most adverse events were mild or moderate, and the companies describe the safety profile as favorable.

p: The companies say they will review the results with the FDA and discuss faster regulatory routes with health authorities. They also plan to present detailed results at a medical meeting and submit them for peer-reviewed publication. Until that happens, the numbers come from a company announcement and have not been independently reviewed.

sections.h: Why it matters for people with ALS
p: Only a small share of people with ALS have a known inherited cause, so this result applies to a limited group. It is still significant for the field: it is the first successful trial in FUS-ALS, and it adds support for the idea that treating the genetic cause of a form of ALS can work. Researchers are testing similar approaches for other ALS genes. Treatments for the most common, non-inherited forms of ALS remain a separate and unsolved challenge.

faq.q: Is there a cure for ALS?
faq.a: No. ALS has no cure today. Ulefnersen is an investigational treatment for one genetic form, FUS-ALS, and has not been approved by the FDA.

faq.q: Can people with FUS-ALS get ulefnersen now?
faq.a: It is not approved. The companies say they are discussing next steps with regulators and the trial's open-label extension continues. People with FUS-ALS should ask their neurologist about genetic testing and about trials or access programs.
